newsitem.title: USA: NBC to offer interactive TV shows in fall.
newsitem.headline: NBC to offer interactive TV shows in fall.

text.p: Making its first foray into the long-hyped world of interactive television, General Electric Co.'s NBC unit said Monday it will offer interactivity in its fall programme schedule.

NBC said it signed a deal to use the interactive technology of privately held Wink Communications on its prime-time entertainment, weekend sports and other programming. Interactive broadcasts will be launched in the late summer.
Analysts hailed NBC's plan as the first inexpensive, wide-scale move into interactive TV, but warned that widespread availability was years away.
"It's an exciting development, the first viable launch of interactive TV on a broad-scale basis that we've seen," said Cynthia Brumfield, a senior analyst at Paul Kagan Associates.
But analysts warned that previous interactive efforts by other companies have failed to prove consumer demand.
The technology will allow viewers to get plot summaries, profiles of athletes, actors and other programme participants, sports scores and other statistics, and answer trivia quizzes.
For example, viewers of a situation comedy such as "Seinfeld" could conceivably get more information on actors in the show by clicking on an interactive icon, or could take a quiz on plot trivia.
NBC will also have interactive advertising. An automobile company could be able to provide brochures about a car and the location of the nearest dealer, for example.
The interactive segments and icons will overlap the screen image. Viewers can interact by using their cable TV set-top boxes and remote controls.
The technology can also be accessed via a specially equipped television. Analysts expect most of NBC's interactive viewers will come via cable.

Wink is testing the system with various U.S. cable systems, and expects about 800,000 U.S. cable subscribers to be interactive by the end of this year. Another 4 million subscribers will be added by the end of 1998, Wink said.
Wink said no TV sets in the United States are equipped with the interactive software at this point, but about 1 million sets will have the feature by the end of 1998.

Wink has made deals with Sony Corp., Toshiba Corp. and JVC to market TV sets to include the software. Matsushita Electric Industrial Co. Ltd said it will ship Wink-enabled Panasonic products later this year.

Several companies, including Time Warner Inc. and Bell Atlantic Corp., ventured into interactive TV, but were faced with large capital investments and lukewarm viewer interest. Analysts said the NBC plan would not require massive capital investments.

NBC was optimistic about revenue possibilities. Peg Murphy, manager of NBC strategic business development, said the network expects a trickle of revenues at first. By the end of 1998, "It's really going to start to have an impact," Murphy said. She declined to elaborate.

Wink Communications was founded in 1995 to focus on interactivity for mass-market consumer electronics. Investors included General Instrument Corp., Scientific-Atlanta Inc., Toshiba, Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp. and Benchmark Capital.
